paras: The Grand Haven jail mob of 1881 was an attempted lynching in June 1881, when a dozen or more farmers broke into the jail at Grand Haven, Ottawa County, Michigan, to hang a prisoner named Voskamp who was accused of murder. The sheriff's wife locked the mob inside the jail, and seven of its leaders later pleaded guilty to assault and were fined $100 each. Newspapers across the country told it as a comic story about lynchers who were themselves captured.

Voskamp, whose name was also printed Vaskamp and Voscamp, was accused of shooting his employer, Lyman H. Cady, at Lamont in the spring of 1881. According to the Chicago Tribune, the shooting followed a quarrel over pay and took place in front of Cady's family. No report gives Voskamp's race.

This was not the first attempt on the prisoner. In May 1881 a crowd of about 250 men from Berlin, Lamont and Allendale came down the river by boat to Grand Haven to lynch him, but Governor Jerome had ordered Company F of the state militia to the jail by telegraph. Faced with some forty armed militiamen in the jail yard, the crowd sailed back at about one o'clock on Sunday morning.

One night in the week before 29 June, with the sheriff away from town, a party of farmers appeared at the jail, overpowered a deputy sheriff and forced him to give up the keys to the prisoner's cell. The New Ulm Weekly Review put their number at 'a score', the Eaton Democrat at 'a dozen or more'. The men all went inside to reach the prisoner and left the outer door unguarded.

Woken by the noise, the sheriff's wife went to the jail, saw what was happening and shut the outer door on the whole party. She then sent her servant girl to ring the fire alarm at the courthouse, and the mob, described as 'respectable farmers', was secured within minutes. The prisoner was not harmed.

Voskamp's murder trial was moved out of Ottawa County on a change of venue granted because of the mob, and it opened in early December 1881 with a plea of insanity. By February 1882 seven men who had led the mob had pleaded guilty to assault and been fined $100 each. One of them was a village physician, and all were described as 'men of good standing'. The outcome of Voskamp's trial does not appear in the coverage.

The first reports, in late June 1881, treated the night as a joke on the would-be lynchers. The New Ulm Weekly Review called it 'a ludicrous scrape' and said the sheriff's wife invited the townspeople 'to come and see the game she had bagged', while the Eaton Democrat ran it under the headline 'Lynchers Captured'. Both papers called the prisoner 'the murderer' or 'a murderer' before any trial.

In February 1882 a short paragraph about the fines ran almost word for word in papers in Nevada, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia and Mississippi. It began 'Lynching is not so popular in Ottawa county, Mich., as in many parts of the West', setting the fines against mob rule elsewhere. When the Clarke Courier of Berryville, Virginia, reprinted it in May 1882, 'last summer' had become 'recently'.

bases: A group of farmers entered the Grand Haven jail and took the cell keys in order to lynch a prisoner accused of murder, but were locked in before they could take him (A2, A3, A5).

The mob of a dozen or more men came to hang a prisoner accused of murder, an illegal act by a group under the pretext of justice, but no one was killed because the sheriff's wife locked them inside the jail (A2, A3, A5).

Two June 1881 reports agree on the jail entry and the sheriff's wife locking in the mob (A2, A3), the Chicago Tribune independently recalls the foiled mob at Voscamp's trial (A4), and a February 1882 paragraph reports the guilty pleas and fines (A5).

accounts.label: Wire report, June 1881
accounts.gist: A dozen or a score of farmers overpowered the deputy and got the cell keys, but the sheriff's wife locked the outer door behind them and had the fire alarm rung, and the mob was captured.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune trial dispatch
accounts.gist: Voscamp had been visited by a mob at Grand Haven that was foiled by the Sheriff's wife, and his trial was moved to another county for that reason.

accounts.label: Follow-up paragraph, 1882
accounts.gist: Seven men who led the mob 'last summer' pleaded guilty to assault and were fined $100 each; one was a village physician.

framing.detail: The June 1881 reports played the episode as a joke on the mob ('a ludicrous scrape', 'the game she had bagged', headline 'Lynchers Captured') while calling the prisoner 'the murderer' and the mob 'respectable farmers'.
The 1882 follow-up contrasted Ottawa county with 'many parts of the West' and stressed the good standing of the men fined.
The follow-up paragraph ran nearly word for word in Nevada, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Georgia and Mississippi papers in February 1882 and again in Virginia in May 1882.

conflicts.note: The seven are described as the leaders, so the figures need not contradict; no report gives an exact count.
